title: What this means for energy traders — Saturday, October 10, 2026

sections.overall: Supply security dominates the week. Hormuz tanker attacks, a Gulf of Mexico hurricane and a US-Russia diesel arrangement all bear on physical availability, while the company-led trends in the ledger are quieter: carbon removal and biochar are gaining participants, and the LNG trends are losing them.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz reached a wartime high, per CNBC, yet Brent fell Friday after Trump said he would pause Iran attacks, per The Guardian. Earlier in the week Brent topped $105 a barrel. Headlines that swing between escalation and restraint are usually read as keeping a risk premium in the market. Hurricane Isaias, which disrupted Gulf output, adds a short-term supply question. Still unclear: how long the pause holds and how much Gulf output is actually offline.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: Isaias also disrupted gas production (Financial Times). On LNG, US weekly exports dropped to 31 cargoes, six fewer than the prior week (LNG Prime). Weather-related export interruptions are typically watched alongside storage data. Both big LNG trends, US export expansion and Asian offtake deals, are FADING on company counts, though the ADNOC and Gulf Development agreement shows contracting continues.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: The Russian diesel deal is the main story, with sanctions-law and political objections reported by CNBC. Added supply is generally read as easing for diesel, but legal challenges and implementation details are unresolved. Shell's expectation of sharply higher refining profit per barrel, per The Guardian, shows how tight the market is.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: Both confirmed carbon trends are RISING. The UK government bought Climeworks credits, and BP's remediation unit picked Myno Carbon for a biochar trial (a company press release). Policy flow continues: the UN market opened to clean cooking projects, and Germany launched a tender for 1.1 million PACM-aligned credits. Retirements are at their highest since 2022 while issuances slid, a mix often read as tightening supply. The EU ETS reform debate remains open.
